html:
A Bronze Age civilisation in what is now Pakistan and northwest India, which lasted from about 3300 to 1300 BCE and was at its height from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. With Egypt and Mesopotamia it was one of the three earliest civilisations of the Old World, and the largest in area.

Its cities are remarkable for their planning. Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi had streets laid out on grids, houses of standard baked bricks, private bathrooms and covered drains. Weights were standard across hundreds of kilometres. Lothal, on the Gujarat coast, may have had a dock.

What we know and what we don't:

  • People grew wheat, barley and cotton, and kept cattle.
  • They traded with Mesopotamia, whose texts seem to call the Indus "Meluhha" and mention its ships in the time of the Akkadian Empire.
  • They carved small stone seals with animals and short inscriptions in the Indus script, which nobody has deciphered.
  • No grand palaces, royal tombs or obvious temples have been found, so we do not know who ruled.
  • Their art includes the bronze Dancing Girl and the "priest-king" bust.

After about 1900 BCE the big cities slowly emptied. Rivers shifted, the Ghaggar-Hakra river system dried up, and the 4.2 kiloyear drought may have weakened the monsoon. People moved east into smaller villages. In the centuries after, Indo-Aryan speakers arrived, and the Vedic period began.

The civilisation was forgotten until excavations at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro in the 1920s.
